claim: Behavior relies on the ability of sensory systems to infer properties of the environment from incoming stimuli.
source: Behavior relies on the ability of sensory systems to infer properties of the environment from incoming stimuli.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract that establishes the premise of the work.

claim: The accuracy of inference depends on the fidelity with which behaviorally relevant properties of stimuli are encoded in neural responses.
source: The accuracy of inference depends on the fidelity with which behaviorally relevant properties of stimuli are encoded in neural responses.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about the relationship between encoding fidelity and inference accuracy.

claim: High-fidelity encodings can be metabolically costly.
source: High-fidelity encodings can be metabolically costly, but low-fidelity encodings can cause errors in inference.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations in the introduction about metabolic costs of encoding.

claim: Low-fidelity encodings can cause errors in inference.
source: High-fidelity encodings can be metabolically costly, but low-fidelity encodings can cause errors in inference.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the consequences of low-fidelity encoding.

claim: Optimal encodings tend to increase the fidelity of the neural representation following a change in the stimulus distribution.
source: These optimal encodings tend to increase the fidelity of the neural representation following a change in the stimulus distribution, and reduce fidelity for stimuli that originate from a known distribution.
evidence: This is a key finding of the work, supported by the theoretical framework and simulations presented.

claim: Optimal encodings reduce fidelity for stimuli that originate from a known distribution.
source: These optimal encodings tend to increase the fidelity of the neural representation following a change in the stimulus distribution, and reduce fidelity for stimuli that originate from a known distribution.
evidence: This is a key finding of the work, supported by the theoretical framework and simulations presented.

claim: Burst coding can be understood as a hallmark of optimal coding for accurate inference.
source: We predict dynamical signatures of such encoding schemes and demonstrate how known phenomena, such as burst coding and firing rate adaptation, can be understood as hallmarks of optimal coding for accurate inference.
evidence: This is a prediction and interpretation based on the theoretical framework developed in the paper.

claim: Firing rate adaptation can be understood as a hallmark of optimal coding for accurate inference.
source: We predict dynamical signatures of such encoding schemes and demonstrate how known phenomena, such as burst coding and firing rate adaptation, can be understood as hallmarks of optimal coding for accurate inference.
evidence: This is a prediction and interpretation based on the theoretical framework developed in the paper.

claim: Color perception can be understood as probabilistic inference.
source: Many perceptual tasks, such as color perception (Brainard et al., 2006), visual speed estimation (Weiss et al., 2002), or sound localization (Fischer and Peña, 2011; Młynarski, 2015), can be understood as probabilistic inference.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Brainard et al., 2006.

claim: Visual speed estimation can be understood as probabilistic inference.
source: Many perceptual tasks, such as color perception (Brainard et al., 2006), visual speed estimation (Weiss et al., 2002), or sound localization (Fischer and Peña, 2011; Młynarski, 2015), can be understood as probabilistic inference.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Weiss et al., 2002.

claim: Sound localization can be understood as probabilistic inference.
source: Many perceptual tasks, such as color perception (Brainard et al., 2006), visual speed estimation (Weiss et al., 2002), or sound localization (Fischer and Peña, 2011; Młynarski, 2015), can be understood as probabilistic inference.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Fischer and Peña, 2011 and Młynarski, 2015.

claim: The nervous system can construct an internal model that relates incoming sensory stimuli to behaviorally relevant properties of the environment.
source: To accurately perform inference, the nervous system can construct an internal model that relates incoming sensory stimuli to behaviorally relevant properties of the environment (Kersten and Schrater, 2002; Kersten et al., 2004; Fiser et al., 2010; Rao et al., 2002; Coen-Cagli et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: As the environment changes, the internal model must be continually updated with new stimuli.
source: As the environment changes, this internal model must be continually updated with new stimuli (Wark et al., 2009; DeWeese and Zador, 1998; Nassar et al., 2010; Lochmann et al., 2012; Deneve, 2008), and therefore the accuracy of this internal model depends on the fidelity with which incoming stimuli are encoded in neural responses.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The accuracy of the internal model depends on the fidelity with which incoming stimuli are encoded in neural responses.
source: As the environment changes, this internal model must be continually updated with new stimuli (Wark et al., 2009; DeWeese and Zador, 1998; Nassar et al., 2010; Lochmann et al., 2012; Deneve, 2008), and therefore the accuracy of this internal model depends on the fidelity with which incoming stimuli are encoded in neural responses.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the need to update the internal model.

claim: The process of encoding sensory stimuli is metabolically expensive.
source: The process of encoding sensory stimuli, however, is metabolically expensive (Laughlin et al., 1998; Mehta and Schwab, 2012; Balasubramanian et al., 2001; Harris et al., 2012; Attwell and Laughlin, 2001; Levy and Baxter, 1996), and a large body of evidence suggests that sensory systems have evolved to reduce the energetic costs of stimulus coding (Laughlin et al., 1998; Laughlin and Sejnowski, 2003; Hermundstad et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: A large body of evidence suggests that sensory systems have evolved to reduce the energetic costs of stimulus coding.
source: The process of encoding sensory stimuli, however, is metabolically expensive (Laughlin et al., 1998; Mehta and Schwab, 2012; Balasubramanian et al., 2001; Harris et al., 2012; Attwell and Laughlin, 2001; Levy and Baxter, 1996), and a large body of evidence suggests that sensory systems have evolved to reduce the energetic costs of stimulus coding (Laughlin et al., 1998; Laughlin and Sejnowski, 2003; Hermundstad et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The efficient coding hypothesis postulates that sensory systems minimize metabolic cost while maximizing the amount of information that is encoded about a stimulus.
source: These findings provide empirical support for the efficient coding hypothesis (Barlow, 1961), which postulates that sensory systems minimize metabolic cost while maximizing the amount of information that is encoded about a stimulus (van Hateren, 1992; Olshausen and Field, 1996; Laughlin, 1981).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the efficient coding hypothesis and related work.

claim: The goal of maximizing stimulus information does not reflect the fact that different stimuli can have different utility to a system for making inferences about the environment.
source: The goal of maximizing stimulus information does not reflect the fact that different stimuli can have different utility to a system for making inferences about the environment (Tishby et al., 2000; Palmer et al., 2015; Geisler et al., 2009; Burge and Geisler, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: The relative utility of a stimulus is determined by the potential impact that it can have on the system's belief about the state of the environment.
source: The relative utility of a stimulus is determined by the potential impact that it can have on the system's belief about the state of the environment; stimuli that sway this belief carry high utility, while stimuli that do not affect this belief are less relevant.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about how utility is determined.

claim: Stimuli that sway the system's belief carry high utility.
source: The relative utility of a stimulus is determined by the potential impact that it can have on the system's belief about the state of the environment; stimuli that sway this belief carry high utility, while stimuli that do not affect this belief are less relevant.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about utility.

claim: Stimuli that do not affect the system's belief are less relevant.
source: The relative utility of a stimulus is determined by the potential impact that it can have on the system's belief about the state of the environment; stimuli that sway this belief carry high utility, while stimuli that do not affect this belief are less relevant.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about relevance.

claim: Physically different stimuli can exert the same influence on the observer's belief and can therefore be encoded in the same neural activity pattern without affecting the inference process.
source: Moreover, physically different stimuli can exert the same influence the observer's belief and can therefore be encoded in the same neural activity pattern without affecting the inference process.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim about encoding strategies.

claim: Encoding physically different stimuli in the same neural activity pattern decreases the fidelity of the neural representation.
source: Such an encoding strategy decreases the fidelity of the neural representation by using the same activity pattern to represent many stimuli, and consequently reduces the amount of metabolic resources required to perform inference.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the encoding strategy described.

claim: Encoding physically different stimuli in the same neural activity pattern reduces the amount of metabolic resources required to perform inference.
source: Such an encoding strategy decreases the fidelity of the neural representation by using the same activity pattern to represent many stimuli, and consequently reduces the amount of metabolic resources required to perform inference.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the encoding strategy described.

claim: When the distribution of stimuli changes in time, both the belief about the environment and the relative impact of different stimuli on this belief also change in time.
source: When the distribution of stimuli changes in time, as in any natural environment, both the belief about the environment (DeWeese and Zador, 1998) and the relative impact of different stimuli on this belief also change in time.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and logical inference.

claim: Any system that must perform accurate inference with minimal energy must dynamically balance the cost of encoding stimuli with the error that this encoding can introduce in the inference process.
source: Any system that must perform accurate inference with minimal energy must therefore dynamically balance the cost of encoding stimuli with the error that this encoding can introduce in the inference process.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the preceding claims about changing stimulus distributions.

claim: Studies have separately shown that sensory neurons dynamically adapt to changing stimulus distributions in manners that reflect optimal encoding.
source: While studies have separately shown that sensory neurons dynamically adapt to changing stimulus distributions in manners that reflect either optimal encoding (Fairhall et al., 2001) or inference (Wark et al., 2009), the interplay between these two objectives is not understood.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fairhall et al., 2001.

claim: Studies have separately shown that sensory neurons dynamically adapt to changing stimulus distributions in manners that reflect optimal inference.
source: While studies have separately shown that sensory neurons dynamically adapt to changing stimulus distributions in manners that reflect either optimal encoding (Fairhall et al., 2001) or inference (Wark et al., 2009), the interplay between these two objectives is not understood.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wark et al., 2009.

claim: The interplay between optimal encoding and inference is not understood.
source: While studies have separately shown that sensory neurons dynamically adapt to changing stimulus distributions in manners that reflect either optimal encoding (Fairhall et al., 2001) or inference (Wark et al., 2009), the interplay between these two objectives is not understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Encoding schemes optimized for inference differ significantly from encoding schemes that are designed to accurately reconstruct all details of the stimulus.
source: We find that encoding schemes optimized for inference differ significantly from encoding schemes that are designed to accurately reconstruct all details of the stimulus.
evidence: This is a key finding of the work, supported by the simulations and analyses presented.

claim: Encoding schemes designed to accurately reconstruct all details of the stimulus produce neural responses that are more metabolically costly.
source: The latter produce neural responses that are more metabolically costly, and the resulting inference process exhibits qualitatively different inaccuracies.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations presented in the paper.

claim: Encoding schemes designed to accurately reconstruct all details of the stimulus result in an inference process that exhibits qualitatively different inaccuracies.
source: The latter produce neural responses that are more metabolically costly, and the resulting inference process exhibits qualitatively different inaccuracies.
evidence: This is a finding from the simulations presented in the paper.

claim: When the observer is certain and the stimulus is expected, the stimulus has a small impact on the observer's estimate.
source: In contrast, when the observer is certain and the stimulus is expected, the stimulus has a small impact on the observer's estimate (schematic (2)).
evidence: This claim is demonstrated using a Bayesian estimation example and illustrated in Figure 1B.

claim: When the observer is certain, a large number of stimuli can be mapped onto the same neural response without inducing error into the observer's estimate.
source: When the observer is certain, a large number of stimuli can be mapped onto the same neural response without inducing error into the observer's estimate (orange panel).
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: When the observer is uncertain, the same mapping from stimulus to response induces higher error.
source: When the observer is uncertain, the same mapping from stimulus to response induces higher error (red panel).
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Error is highest when mapping a surprising stimulus onto an expected neural response, or vice versa.
source: Error is highest when mapping a surprising stimulus onto an expected neural response, or vice versa.
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 1C.

claim: Stimuli have a larger impact on the observer's estimate when the observer is uncertain and when stimuli are unexpected.
source: Stimuli have a larger impact on the observer's estimate when the observer is uncertain and when stimuli are unexpected (quantified by surprise in the case of location estimation, and centered surprise in the case of scale estimation; see main text).
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 1D for different stimulus distributions.

claim: The error induced by mapping a stimulus onto a response grows with the surprise of the stimulus.
source: The error induced by mapping a stimulus onto a response grows with the surprise of the stimulus.
evidence: This claim is illustrated in Figure 1D.

claim: The optimal encoder devotes its resolution to stimuli that are surprising given the current prediction of the environment when designed for accurate inference.
source: When designed for accurate inference, we find that the optimal encoder devotes its resolution to stimuli that are surprising given the current prediction of the environment (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is a key finding illustrated in Figure 3B.

claim: When the observer's prediction is accurate, the bulk of the stimulus distribution is mapped onto the same response level, and entropy rates are low.
source: As a result, when the observer's prediction is accurate, the bulk of the stimulus distribution is mapped onto the same response level (Figure 3B, left), and entropy rates are low (blue curve in Figure 3D, left).
evidence: This is a finding from the discretization encoding scheme, illustrated in Figures 3B and 3D.

claim: When the environment changes abruptly, the bulk of the new stimulus distribution is mapped onto different response levels, resulting in a large spike in entropy rate.
source: When the environment changes abruptly, the bulk of the new stimulus distribution is mapped onto different response levels. This results in a large spike in entropy rate, which enables the observer to quickly adapt its estimate to the change (blue curve in Figure 3E, left).
evidence: This is a finding from the discretization encoding scheme, illustrated in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: The optimal encoder devotes its resolution to stimuli that are likely given the current prediction of the environmental state when designed for accurate reconstruction of the stimulus.
source: When designed for accurate reconstruction of the stimulus, we find that the optimal encoder devotes its resolution to stimuli that are likely given the current prediction of the environmental state (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a finding illustrated in Figure 3C.

claim: Entropy rates are high when the observer's prediction is accurate for encoders optimized for stimulus reconstruction, regardless of the environment.
source: As a result, entropy rates are high when the observer's prediction is accurate, regardless of the environment (green curves in Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a finding from the discretization encoding scheme optimized for reconstruction, illustrated in Figure 3D.

claim: Entropy rates drop when the environment changes for encoders optimized for stimulus reconstruction, because likely stimuli become mapped onto the same response level.
source: Entropy rates drop when the environment changes, because likely stimuli become mapped onto the same response level. This drop slows the observer's detection of changes in the environment (green curve in Figure 3E, left).
evidence: This is a finding from the discretization encoding scheme optimized for reconstruction, illustrated in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: A strategy optimized for inference achieves lower inference error than a strategy optimized for stimulus reconstruction across all numbers of response levels.
source: As expected, a strategy optimized for inference achieves lower inference error than a strategy optimized for stimulus reconstruction (across all numbers of response levels), but it also does so at significantly lower coding cost.
evidence: This is a key finding illustrated in Figure 3F.

claim: A strategy optimized for inference achieves lower inference error at significantly lower coding cost than a strategy optimized for stimulus reconstruction.
source: As expected, a strategy optimized for inference achieves lower inference error than a strategy optimized for stimulus reconstruction (across all numbers of response levels), but it also does so at significantly lower coding cost.
evidence: This is a key finding illustrated in Figure 3F.

claim: Filters optimized for inference devote high fidelity at times when the observer is uncertain and stimuli are predicted to be surprising.
source: When designed for accurate inference, we find that the optimal encoder devotes higher fidelity at times when the observer is uncertain and the predicted stimulus variance is high.
evidence: This is a finding from the temporal filtering encoding scheme, illustrated in Figure 4B.

claim: In a mean-switching environment, the stimulus variance is fixed, and thus the fidelity depends only on the observer's uncertainty.
source: In a mean-switching environment, the stimulus variance is fixed (Figure 4A, left), and thus the fidelity depends only on the observer's uncertainty.
evidence: This is an observation from the temporal filtering encoding scheme in a mean-switching environment.

claim: Uncertainty grows rapidly following a change in the environment, which results in a transient increase in coding fidelity and a rapid adaptation of the observer's estimate.
source: This uncertainty grows rapidly following a change in the environment, which results in a transient increase in coding fidelity (Figure 4B, left) and a rapid adaptation of the observer's estimate (Figure 4D, left).
evidence: This is a finding from the temporal filtering encoding scheme, illustrated in Figures 4B and 4D.

claim: In a variance-switching environment, the predicted stimulus variance changes in time, resulting in an additional increase in fidelity when the environment is in the high- versus low-variance state.
source: In a variance-switching environment, the predicted stimulus variance also changes in time (Figure 4A, right). This results in an additional increase in fidelity when the environment is in the high- versus low-variance state, and an asymmetry between the filter responses for downward versus upward switches in variance (Figure 4B, right).
evidence: This is a finding from the temporal filtering encoding scheme in a variance-switching environment, illustrated in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: Both the encoder and the observer are slower to respond to changes in variance than to changes in mean.
source: Both the encoder and the observer are slower to respond to changes in variance than to changes in mean, and the accuracy of the inference is more sensitive to the strength of the entropy constraint (Figure 4D, right).
evidence: This is a finding from the temporal filtering encoding scheme, illustrated in Figure 4D.

claim: The accuracy of the inference is more sensitive to the strength of the entropy constraint for variance estimation than for mean estimation.
source: Both the encoder and the observer are slower to respond to changes in variance than to changes in mean, and the accuracy of the inference is more sensitive to the strength of the entropy constraint (Figure 4D, right).
evidence: This is a finding from the temporal filtering encoding scheme, illustrated in Figure 4D.

claim: When designed to accurately reconstruct the stimulus, the fidelity of the optimal encoder depends only on the predicted stimulus variance.
source: When designed to accurately reconstruct the stimulus, the fidelity of the optimal encoder depends only on the predicted stimulus variance.
evidence: This is a finding from the temporal filtering encoding scheme optimized for reconstruction.

claim: In a mean-switching environment, the variance is fixed, and thus the fidelity is flat across time for encoders optimized for reconstruction.
source: In a mean-switching environment, the variance is fixed (Figure 4A), and thus the fidelity is flat across time.
evidence: This is a finding from the temporal filtering encoding scheme optimized for reconstruction, illustrated in Figure 4C.

claim: In a variance-switching environment, the fidelity increases with the predicted variance of incoming stimuli for encoders optimized for reconstruction, not because variable stimuli are more surprising, but rather because they are larger in magnitude and can lead to higher errors in reconstruction.
source: In a variance-switching environment, the fidelity increases with the predicted variance of incoming stimuli, not because variable stimuli are more surprising, but rather because they are larger in magnitude and can lead to higher errors in reconstruction (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a finding from the temporal filtering encoding scheme optimized for reconstruction, illustrated in Figure 4C.

claim: When the mean of the stimulus distribution changes in time, very few stimuli are required to maintain an accurate estimate of the environmental state.
source: When the mean of the stimulus distribution changes in time, very few stimuli are required to maintain an accurate estimate of the environmental state (Figure 5A–B, left).
evidence: This is a finding from the stimulus selection encoding scheme, illustrated in Figures 5A-B.

claim: When the environment changes abruptly, the observer's prediction is no longer aligned with the environment, and the misalignment signal increases until incoming stimuli are encoded and used to adapt the observer's prediction.
source: When the environment changes abruptly, the observer's prediction is no longer aligned with the environment, and the misalignment signal increases until incoming stimuli are encoded and used to adapt the observer's prediction.
evidence: This is a finding from the stimulus selection encoding scheme, illustrated in Figure 5A.

claim: There is a delay between the switch in the environment and the burst of encoded stimuli, which is proportional to the size of the threshold.
source: Because it requires several stimulus samples for the misalignment to exceed threshold, there is a delay between the switch in the environment and the burst of encoded stimuli. This delay, which is proportional to the size of the threshold, slows the observer's detection of the change (Figure 5C, left).
evidence: This is a finding from the stimulus selection encoding scheme, illustrated in Figure 5C.

claim: When the variance abruptly increases, the misalignment signal grows both because the observer's prediction is no longer accurate, and because the average surprise of the incoming stimulus distribution increases.
source: When the variance abruptly increases, the misalignment signal grows both because the observer's prediction is no longer accurate, and because the average surprise of the incoming stimulus distribution increases.
evidence: This is an explanation of the behavior of the stimulus selection encoding scheme in a variance-switching environment.

claim: A large proportion of stimuli are transmitted when the variance abruptly increases, and the observer quickly adapts to the change.
source: A large proportion of stimuli are transmitted, and the observer quickly adapts to the change.
evidence: This is a finding from the stimulus selection encoding scheme in a variance-switching environment.

claim: If the threshold is sufficiently high, the observer's prediction never fully aligns with the true state when the variance abruptly increases.
source: If the threshold is sufficiently high, however, the observer's prediction never fully aligns with the true state.
evidence: This is a finding from the stimulus selection encoding scheme, illustrated in Figure 5C.

claim: When the variance abruptly decreases, the incoming stimulus distribution is less surprising on average, and therefore a greater number of stimulus samples is needed before the misalignment signal exceeds threshold.
source: When the variance abruptly decreases, the incoming stimulus distribution is less surprising on average, and therefore a greater number of stimulus samples is needed before the misalignment signal exceeds threshold.
evidence: This is an explanation of the behavior of the stimulus selection encoding scheme when variance decreases.

claim: The observer is slower to detect decreases in variance than increases.
source: As a result, the observer is slower to detect decreases in variance than increases (Figure 5C, right).
evidence: This is a finding from the stimulus selection encoding scheme, illustrated in Figure 5C.

claim: Encodings optimized for inference typically show transient changes in neural response properties after a switch in the environment, followed by a return to baseline.
source: We find that encodings optimized for inference typically show transient changes in neural response properties after a switch in the environment, followed by a return to baseline.
evidence: This is a general finding illustrated in Figure 6A-C.

claim: Transient changes in neural response properties are manifested in a burst in firing rates in the case of discretization, and a burst in response variability in the cases of filtering and stimulus selection.
source: This is manifested in a burst in firing rates in the case of discretization, and a burst in response variability in the cases of filtering and stimulus selection.
evidence: This is a finding illustrated in Figure 6A-C.

claim: Filtering is additionally marked by a transient decrease in the temporal correlation of the response.
source: Filtering is additionally marked by a transient decrease in the temporal correlation of the response.
evidence: This is a finding illustrated in Figure 6B.

claim: The magnitude of transient changes relative to baseline is most apparent in the case of mean estimation, where the variability in the environment remains fixed over time.
source: The magnitude of these transient changes relative to baseline is most apparent in the case of mean estimation, where the variability in the environment remains fixed over time.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulations illustrated in Figure 6A-C.

claim: Baseline response properties change during variance estimation, and bursts relative to baseline are less pronounced.
source: Because periods of higher variability in the environment are intrinsically more surprising, baseline response properties change during variance estimation, and bursts relative to baseline are less pronounced.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulations illustrated in Figure 6A-C.

claim: For mean estimation, firing rates and response variability remain nearly constant over time for encoders optimized for stimulus reconstruction, despite abrupt changes in the mean of the stimulus distribution.
source: For mean estimation, firing rates and response variability remain nearly constant over time, despite abrupt changes in the mean of the stimulus distribution.
evidence: This is a finding from encoders optimized for reconstruction, illustrated in Figure 6A-C.

claim: Discretization shows a brief rise and dip in firing rate following a switch, which has been observed experimentally.
source: Discretization shows a brief rise and dip in firing rate following a switch, which has been observed experimentally (Fairhall et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a finding from the discretization encoding scheme optimized for reconstruction, with a citation to experimental work.

claim: For variance estimation, response properties show sustained (rather than transient) changes following a switch for encoders optimized for reconstruction.
source: For variance estimation, response properties show sustained (rather than transient) changes following a switch.
evidence: This is a finding from encoders optimized for reconstruction, illustrated in Figure 6A-C.

claim: Both the speed and accuracy of inference are symmetric to changes in the mean of the stimulus distribution, but asymmetric to changes in variance.
source: We find that both the speed and accuracy of inference are symmetric to changes in the mean of the stimulus distribution, but asymmetric to changes in variance.
evidence: This is a finding illustrated in Figure 6D-E.

claim: Encoding schemes optimized for inference have a more significant impact on the speed and accuracy of variance estimation than of mean estimation.
source: We find that encoding schemes optimized for inference have a more significant impact on the speed and accuracy of variance estimation than of mean estimation.
evidence: This is a finding illustrated in Figure 6D-E.

claim: In the absence of encoding, the ideal observer is faster to respond to increases than to decreases in variance.
source: In the absence of encoding, the ideal observer is faster to respond to increases than to decreases in variance.
evidence: This is a finding about the ideal observer, illustrated in Figure 6E.

claim: Encoding via stimulus selection increases the asymmetry in response speed to increases versus decreases in variance.
source: We find that encoding via stimulus selection increases this asymmetry, encoding via discretization nearly removes this asymmetry, and encoding via stimulus selection reverses this asymmetry.
evidence: This is a finding illustrated in Figure 6E.

claim: Encoding via discretization nearly removes the asymmetry in response speed to increases versus decreases in variance.
source: We find that encoding via stimulus selection increases this asymmetry, encoding via discretization nearly removes this asymmetry, and encoding via stimulus selection reverses this asymmetry.
evidence: This is a finding illustrated in Figure 6E.

claim: Encoding via temporal filtering reverses the asymmetry in response speed to increases versus decreases in variance.
source: We find that encoding via stimulus selection increases this asymmetry, encoding via discretization nearly removes this asymmetry, and encoding via stimulus selection reverses this asymmetry.
evidence: This is a finding illustrated in Figure 6E. Note: The text appears to have a typo, mentioning 'stimulus selection' twice, but the context suggests the third instance should refer to 'temporal filtering'.

claim: Both the dynamics of the neural response and the patterns of deviation from optimal inference could be used to infer features of the underlying sensory coding scheme.
source: Together, these observations suggest that both the dynamics of the neural response and the patterns of deviation from optimal inference could be used to infer features of the underlying sensory coding scheme.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings presented in Figure 6.

claim: An efficient system could prioritize some encoding schemes over others, depending on whether the goal is to reconstruct the stimulus or infer its underlying properties.
source: Moreover, these results suggest that an efficient system could prioritize some encoding schemes over others, depending on whether the goal is to reconstruct the stimulus or infer its underlying properties, and if the latter, whether this goal hinges on speed, accuracy, or both.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings about different encoding schemes.

claim: Individual image patches have a large impact on the observer's estimate when the observer is uncertain and when image patches have high centered surprise.
source: Individual image patches have a large impact on the observer's estimate when the observer is uncertain and when image patches have high centered surprise, analogous to the behavior observed in simple model environments (see Figure 1B).
evidence: This is a finding from the natural image simulation, illustrated in Figure 7D.

claim: The observer can exploit its uncertainty to adapt the sparsity of the sensory encoding.
source: The observer can exploit its uncertainty to adapt the sparsity of the sensory encoding (heatmap; blue trace).
evidence: This is a finding from the natural image simulation, illustrated in Figure 7E.

claim: When the observer is certain, population activity can be significantly reduced without changing the inference error.
source: When the observer is certain (white marker), population activity can be significantly reduced without changing the inference error.
evidence: This is a finding from the natural image simulation, illustrated in Figure 7E.

claim: Increases in uncertainty result in bursts of activity.
source: Increases in uncertainty (red marker) result in bursts of activity (red bar).
evidence: This is a finding from the natural image simulation, illustrated in Figure 7E.

claim: An encoder optimized for constant reconstruction error produces activity that remains constant over time.
source: An encoder optimized for constant reconstruction error produces activity that remains constant over time (green trace).
evidence: This is a finding from the natural image simulation, illustrated in Figure 7E.

claim: The observer can exploit the predicted surprise of incoming stimuli to reduce population activity when stimuli are expected.
source: The observer can similarly exploit the predicted surprise of incoming stimuli to reduce population activity when stimuli are expected.
evidence: This is a finding from the natural image simulation, illustrated in Figure 7F.

claim: Surprising stimuli that project strongly on curvature filters exert a large impact on inference.
source: Surprising stimuli that project strongly on curvature filters exert a large impact on inference, while expected stimuli (characterized by low centered surprise) exert little impact (Figure 7C–D, F).
evidence: This is a finding from the natural image simulation, illustrated in Figures 7C-D and 7F.

claim: Expected stimuli characterized by low centered surprise exert little impact on inference.
source: Surprising stimuli that project strongly on curvature filters exert a large impact on inference, while expected stimuli (characterized by low centered surprise) exert little impact (Figure 7C–D, F).
evidence: This is a finding from the natural image simulation, illustrated in Figures 7C-D and 7F.

claim: Individual stimuli exert a larger impact on the estimate when the observer is uncertain than when the observer is certain.
source: Similarly, individual stimuli exert a larger impact on the estimate when the observer is uncertain than when the observer is certain (Figure 7D–E).
evidence: This is a finding from the natural image simulation, illustrated in Figures 7D-E.

claim: Similar population bursts were recently observed in V1 in response to violations of statistical regularities in stimulus sequences.
source: Similar population bursts were recently observed in V1 in response to violations of statistical regularities in stimulus sequences (Homann et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Homann et al., 2017.

claim: When the environment is changing over time, the relative utility of incoming stimuli for inference can also change.
source: First, when the environment is changing over time, the relative utility of incoming stimuli for inference can also change.
evidence: This is a general principle identified in the discussion.

claim: Physically different signals can exert similar influence on the observer's model of the environment and can therefore be encoded in the same neural representation without negatively affecting the inference process.
source: Second, physically different signals can exert similar influence on the observer's model of the environment and can therefore be encoded in the same neural representation without negatively affecting the inference process.
evidence: This is a general principle identified in the discussion.

claim: When the goal is accurate inference, the encoder can optimally adapt depending on the uncertainty in the observer's belief about the state of the environment, and on the surprise of incoming stimuli given this belief.
source: We demonstrated that when the goal is accurate inference, the encoder can optimally adapt depending on the uncertainty in the observer's belief about the state of the environment, and on the surprise of incoming stimuli given this belief.
evidence: This is a key finding summarized in the discussion.

claim: Optimal adaptation enables the system to efficiently infer high-level features from low-level inputs.
source: This optimal adaptation enables the system to efficiently infer high-level features from low-level inputs, which we argue is a broad goal of neural circuits across the brain.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of the work.

claim: Inferring high-level features from low-level inputs is a broad goal of neural circuits across the brain.
